title: “Dual Fuel Heat Pumps are JUNK” 😬🔥
summary: HVAC contractor defends dual-fuel heat pumps: cold-climate heating loads exceed cooling loads and duct capacity, so a small heat pump plus furnace backup makes sense.

assertions.quote: I can almost guarantee the duct work is not big enough to handle this amount of air flow

verdicts.note: Heat pumps need about 400 cfm/ton versus about 156 for non-condensing furnaces because of cooler supply air, and one expert estimates most duct systems handle only 2-3 tons of airflow.
At Site 7 undersized return ductwork caused low COP and excess auxiliary heat; rebuilding the return plenum raised capacity, though COP stayed below expected.
76% of installs needed some duct upgrades and 29% major ones, which drove up price, but the report does not say whether undersized ducts for airflow were the reason.

In field-tested retrofit systems, 53% had coil airflow below 350 cfm per ton; the authors attribute the worst airflow partly to older California homes whose ducts were likely designed for heating only and undersized for cooling (an inference, not a duct sizing test).

assertions.quote: an air source heat pump is just an air conditioner with a reversing valve

verdicts.note: The paper describes heat pumps as reversible air conditioners that reverse refrigerant flow in winter to move outdoor heat inside.
The paper refers to air conditioners as one-way heat pumps, contrasting them with two-way heat pumps sized for heating.
RMI describes heat pumps as working like air conditioners in summer and running in reverse in winter, so an air conditioner is the one-direction case.
Describes the heat pump in cooling mode as running the cycle in the opposite direction, removing indoor heat like a traditional air conditioner; a descriptive statement, not a measurement.
Describes heat pumps as fully reversible, working the same way as a cooler in warm weather by removing heat from indoors, which matches the idea of an air conditioner that also runs in reverse.

assertions.quote: heat pumps will not be able to carry the entire load of a house in cold climates

verdicts.note: Single-speed units sized to cooling load fall short at design temperature, but variable-speed cold-climate units can be upsized for heating without short-cycling.

The minimum-efficiency unit sized for the cooling load has a much smaller heating capacity and relies on resistance heat when it cannot meet the load; design heating loads exceed cooling loads in about 70% of homes.
Sizing for heating added about one ton over cooling sizing; for an example home a 2-ton (cooling-sized) unit would hand off to the furnace at 27F versus 14F for 3-ton and 5F for 4-ton.

assertions.quote: that 2ton heat pump will keep up with the heating load the majority of the time in Denver

verdicts.note: Most heating hours occur at mild temperatures, so a heat pump sized below the design load still covers most of the season's heat.
Citing Waite and Modi, with dual-source heat pumps only 1-2% of heating energy may need to come from natural gas.
With a properly sized ccASHP the backup furnace is expected to meet under 30% of the heating load, so a cheaper 80% AFUE furnace suffices since it runs only a small portion of the season.

assertions.quote: the system is going to be way oversized for the house and short cycle in cooling season

verdicts.note: Site 8, undersized because of an inefficient distribution system, relied on resistance heat for about 20% of the load and ran it after every defrost, significantly lowering performance; oversizing was not the problem seen in this sample.

Units from one contractor with sloppy installs (up to 30 ft of excess coiled line set) ran 0.5-1.0 lower in COP at all temperatures, which rated efficiency cannot explain; the report adds that cooling oversizing of variable-speed units should not appreciably hurt efficiency.

Side-by-side lab homes with a two-stage heat pump: imposed duct leakage raised cooling energy 17-25% and lost indoor temperature and humidity control at peak, and combined faults (undercharge, duct leak, non-condensables) raised cooling energy 38-40%; cooling only, one Florida test facility.

Across 308 metered Florida homes, oversizing carried a modest cooling energy penalty (about 3.7% at 120% of Manual J and 9.3% at 150%) and 13% higher peak demand, but run-time data showed no comfort difference between modestly and heavily oversized units; the comfort problem appeared in undersized ones.

assertions.quote: recommended systems range from 35k up to 60k

verdicts.note: Quote comparisons and program data show installed heat pump prices for similar homes varying by multiples between contractors.
Even after location and inflation corrections, installed costs remain extremely variable, driven in part by pricing strategies and installer experience.

LBNL: the range of costs for almost all measures is very large (interquartile ranges about half the mean or more), driven by building condition, climate and other variables; the data do not isolate contractor-to-contractor spread for identical equipment.
The model adds high upfront-cost sensitivities to reflect the wide variety of contractor quotes consumers receive.
